Artificial Intelligence Advances Biological Digital Twins While Validation Limits Regulatory Adoption

Artificial intelligence is transforming biological digital twins across every level of biological organization, offering a promising pathway to replace animal testing with human-relevant methods, but scientific validation and lifecycle governance remain the primary barriers to regulatory acceptance. In a theoretical analysis published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, toxicologist Thomas Hartung examines how deep learning, transformer architectures, foundation models, and physics-informed neural networks have elevated biological simulation beyond static systems of differential equations. Rather than functioning as generic classifiers or open-loop simulations, biological digital twins maintain internal states coupled to physical counterparts through continuous data assimilation. Across five nested scales, extending from single-cell multi-omics to the environmental exposures of entire populations, these computational architectures show unprecedented capacity to model human biology without surrogate animal species. However, Hartung argues that technical ingenuity alone cannot secure regulatory trust. Without agreed credibility standards, independent prospective testing, and formal governance to oversee self-updating algorithms, biological twins risk becoming expensive computational artifacts that fail in high-stakes clinical and toxicological decisions.

To distinguish authentic biological digital twins from superficial marketing claims, the analysis establishes four foundational commitments that exclude conventional simulations, software dashboards, and static pattern predictors. First, a biological digital twin demands specificity, binding its computational state to a distinct biological instance, such as a single patient or an individual organ-on-chip, rather than an average population category. Second, the framework requires continuous data assimilation, creating an iterative loop where incoming telemetry, biosensor readings, or longitudinal omics samples update the model to track the physical drift of the living system over time. Third, the twin must encode mechanistic constraints derived from biological principles rather than statistical correlations alone, preventing algorithms from predicting biologically impossible outcomes beyond training distributions. Finally, the system demands empirical testability, producing refutable predictions with quantified uncertainty that physical experiments can confirm or overturn. Representations lacking any of these criteria, including frozen neural networks, open-loop simulations, or decorative avatars, fail to meet this definition and cannot serve as dependable regulatory instruments.

At the bottom level of the proposed hierarchy sits the cellular digital twin, where representation learning and foundation models fuse multimodal single-cell measurements into dynamic latent manifolds. Traditional cellular models relied on hand-crafted equations or immortalized rodent lines, failing to capture the high dimensionality and non-linear regulatory networks of human biology. Modern deep-learning architectures, including single-cell foundation models such as Geneformer, scGPT, and scFoundation, learn compressed representations across tens of millions of cellular profiles, separating technical batch artifacts from genuine biological signals. This computational manifold enables virtual perturbation experiments, allowing researchers to simulate how cellular trajectories shift when challenged by novel pharmacological compounds, gene knockouts, or environmental toxicants. In exploratory toxicology, virtual cells reorder experimental pipelines, nominating the most informative hypotheses for bench testing while reducing reliance on early rodent toxicity screens and primary animal cell cultures. However, the analysis clarifies that general foundation models serve as shared infrastructure rather than digital twins until conditioned on specific cell populations and coupled to incoming experimental data.

Ascending to the in vitro level, computational twins model engineered cell cultures, microfluidic devices, and organoids, representing what Hartung identifies as the most technologically mature tier of the ladder. Because laboratory culture systems operate within defined physical geometries, controlled flow rates, and instrumented chambers, mechanistic transport equations can be readily combined with empirical machine learning. For instance, the DigiLoCS liver-on-chip framework explicitly separates intracellular metabolism, passive permeability, and compartment partitioning, predicting clinical drug clearance distributions far more accurately than conventional lumped single-compartment methods. Concurrently, emerging organoid twins incorporate biophysical priors and active learning to forecast therapeutic responses and drug resistance in patient-derived cancer tissues, offering human-relevant alternatives to slow, ethically fraught patient-derived xenograft rodent models. Coupled with laboratory automation, these closed-loop organoid systems can iteratively predict responses, execute robotic perturbations, and update internal states within hours. Nonetheless, mathematical unidentifiability, where multiple unmeasured parameter combinations yield identical observable outputs, remains a persistent technical challenge requiring targeted, standardized physical measurements rather than algorithmic expansion alone.

At the organ level, digital twins confront physiological challenges that lower scales can postpone, including fluid dynamics, biomechanics, barrier transport, and electrical propagation across anatomical structures. To bypass the immense computational cost of traditional finite-element modeling without resorting to large-animal studies in dogs or pigs, investigators are deploying physics-informed neural networks. By penalizing violations of physical conservation laws directly within loss functions, these networks act as rapid surrogate models, executing organ-scale biomechanical simulations in near-real time while maintaining physical plausibility outside training domains. In parallel, multi-organ microphysiological systems combine human tissue chips with computational twins, as illustrated by a three-organ platform linking gut, liver, and placental tissues to investigate maternal-fetal pharmacokinetics during pregnancy. Because reproductive toxicity and placental transfer diverge sharply between rodent models and humans, such human-specific multi-organ twins directly address conditions where animal testing routinely misleads. Derived from the Virtual Physiological Human tradition, these hybrid architectures demonstrate that integrating mechanistic physical principles with machine learning is essential for auditable, trustworthy organ-scale safety assessments.

Progressing to individual human patients, the Virtual Human Twin integrates multimodal health records, wearable telemetry, high-resolution imaging, and personal omics into an individualized clinical forecast. Operating as an exploratory sandbox for precision medicine, personal twins enable clinicians to compare therapeutic regimens, evaluate dosing schedules, and anticipate adverse drug reactions in silico prior to clinical administration. In cardiology, personalized models calibrated to patient-specific electrophysiology and anatomical imaging have successfully simulated arrhythmic activation pathways to guide catheter ablation procedures before surgery. Similarly, in oncology, hybrid twins simulating tumor microenvironments assist clinicians in navigating heterogeneous malignancies without relying on animal xenografts. Nevertheless, the review strongly cautions against ungrounded hype surrounding all-encompassing digital human replicas that claim to forecast a patient’s entire lifespan.
